old: First letter in the collection. Documents the 34th NY's journey from Albany to Washington in the opening weeks of the war, including passage through Baltimore — a city where a riot had killed soldiers just weeks earlier (April 19, 1861).
draft: Henry's first letter home: the 34th New York reaches Washington after marching through Baltimore, where twenty men carried loaded guns "in case of attack" but the city "rather cheered" them. He notes bullet holes in the depot roof from an earlier row. Already mindful of his widowed mother, he declines a costly furlough home, trusting she will need the eight dollars he sent more than he needs the visit.

old: Henry is writing from Washington while hearing the cannons of the First Battle of Bull Run (Manassas) — the first major battle of the Civil War, fought July 21, 1861, approximately 25-30 miles from Washington. This is a real-time eyewitness account of the battle's sound reaching the capital.
draft: Writing from Washington on July 21, 1861, Henry tells his mother that "while I am writing there is a battle going on," with cannons firing "not over twenty-eight miles from here" — a real-time eyewitness account of distant fighting. Uncertain whether his regiment will move or serve as city guard, he steadies himself in faith hours after a six o'clock chapel service, adding that wherever he goes, he is ready.

old: The "Later" postscript is written as news of the Union defeat at First Bull Run reaches Washington. Henry's regiment is ordered to move — the capital is in panic. The shift from mundane daily life ("I want to get a shirt washed") to "There has been a hard battle today" in a single letter is one of the most dramatic moments in the collection.
draft: Writing from Washington, Henry fills most of this letter to his sister Frances with ordinary camp life — five hours of daily drill, the Colonel's praise, two newspapers to read, a request for a dollar to wash a shirt. Then a postscript breaks in: "We are ordered off," a hard battle was fought that day, and he tells her not to send the money after all.

old: Camp life update with details on guard duty along the Potomac and accidental death in regiment.
draft: Writing from the Washington defenses, Henry reports his 34th New York regiment posted as Potomac guards against rebel crossings — and the suspicion it may never see battle, to which he answers, "I for one am willing to go. I don't care where." He sends his five-dollar gold piece home by the Captain, ordering his sister and mother to spend it: "I put that down as a command." A Co. H private, the regiment's third such loss, was killed when soldiers playing with their guns let one go off.

old: References Battle of Hatteras Inlet (Aug 28-29, 1861), Henry's advice against Alexander enlisting, cannon fire into Virginia, and rumor of wintering in Kentucky. Important for Alexander's enlistment timeline.

He has just learned of the fall of Fort Hatteras, "a noble achievement," and wagers the war can't last two years. A P.S. warns that Ransom's company may be "scattered" if he reaches Albany short of a full quota.

old: Confirms Alexander has officially enlisted ("in for the war"). False alarm incident at camp. Money being sent home via Reich.
draft: Henry takes in the news that his brother Alexander has gone "in for the war," answering it with measured resignation — "Perhaps it is all for the best" — and the conviction it cannot last long. From camp near Washington he reports bombs fired over into Virginia and a false alarm in which guards shot at a white horse, even as he prepares to send twenty-five dollars home and heads out on two days' picket.

old: Detailed camp life: tent improvements, guard duty, rations, card-playing ban. Corrects exaggerated report of a skirmish.

He notes the colonel's new ban on card-playing after too much gambling, and admits he held off writing of his illness because he couldn't spell the word.

old: Entire company under arrest over rope-cutting incident. Lt. Scott conflict. Military punishment details. Charles considering enlistment — Henry says join his company if he does. Chaplain sick.
draft: A disciplinary crisis grips Henry's company: a soldier who left his picket early and quarreled with Lt. Scott was punished with docked pay, a 30-lb knapsack, and his hands tied above his head — until a comrade cut the rope, putting the whole company under arrest. Writing from picket duty near Washington, Henry insists he keeps clear of trouble and "tries to do what is right," and notes that his brother Charles is now anxious to enlist.

old: Brigadier General Gormon's inspection; regiment called "sharp shooters" in press. POW escape narrative — Kellogg confirmed prisoner in Richmond. Murder by stabbing in camp. Poolesville winter quarters rumor. James confirmed in school.

Henry also reports a drunken stabbing in camp that killed a man by morning, and Brig. Gen. Gormon's inspection of the 34th, lately dubbed "the sharp shooters" in the papers.

Henry notes the enemy is visible by day and keeps fires along the river at night, with orders forbidding talk across the water.

old: Winter conditions, furlough queue, Thanksgiving on picket, picture taken, farm concerns, tax willingness.
draft: Writing from Camp McClellan in the cold, Henry begs his worrying mother to "let your mind rest at perfect ease," reports he is third or fourth in the furlough queue, and came off picket Thanksgiving day at two o'clock. He confesses he sometimes thinks he "did wrong to leave home" with the farm needing him, yet pledges that "when I do get home I shall stay."
final: Writing from Camp McClellan in cold too sharp to hold a pen, Henry tells his worried mother to "let your mind rest at perfect ease" and reports his furlough is stalled behind three or four others, with the war perhaps over before his turn. He notes with pride that the 34th was called the best-looking regiment to cross the pontoon bridge.

old: March to Winchester and back — 34th NY and two brigades marched 30 miles from Harpers Ferry toward Winchester, found 25,000 Union troops already there. Rebels had left "probably for good.
draft: Henry's regiment and two brigades marched some thirty miles on foot from Harpers Ferry toward Winchester to drive out the rebels, only to learn within three miles of the town that 25,000 Union troops already held it and the Confederates had fled "probably for good." Footsore from picket and skirmish duty, he admits to a "good many hardships" yet hopes nine months from home that the rebellion will be over by next summer.

old: Bell tents detailed: 16 men, bell-shaped stove in center, pole in middle, open top for smoke. Roads to Winchester: macadamized (small stone), very good in any weather.
draft: Writing from Camp Gorman on Bolivar Heights, Henry tells his brother James that the brigade expects to leave soon for Washington, and that the Shenandoah River railroad bridge is repaired so cars again run to Winchester. Amid weather that toppled two tents, he confesses a long-neglected debt for Mrs. Douglas's flour and asks James to pay it from his money — adding, wearily, that he wouldn't object if the war closed next week.

old: 34th NY moves from Harpers Ferry to Washington — 83 miles by freight train in 24 hours. Arrived ~2 AM, marched 1+ mile to brick barracks.
draft: After the railroad bridge at Harpers Ferry was finished, Henry's 34th New York rode a freight train eighty-three miles to Washington in twenty-four hours, reaching brick barracks at 2 a.m. to await pay before an unknown next assignment. He marvels that a Sabbath in the capital feels nothing like one — cars running, drunken soldiers, the provost guard hauling in stragglers — and vows to dodge arrest himself.

old: 34th NY moves to the Peninsula — Alexandria → steamboat → Fortress Monroe → Hampton, VA. ~200 miles in 2 days.
draft: Henry writes from Hampton, Va., after the 34th New York's two-day steamboat passage from Alexandria to Fortress Monroe — nearly 200 miles across a Chesapeake Bay so wide he could see no land on either side. He finds the town burned to the ground, "worse than Harpers Ferry," and the men penned up like sheep, sleeping under rubber blankets buttoned into tents, shrugging off hard crackers and no coffee with a soldier's resignation.

old: Henry keeping a journal — "I have been keeping a Journal some time. " Plans to copy and send home.
draft: Writing by candlelight near Fortress Monroe, Henry tells his mother he has been "keeping a Journal" he means to copy and send home — and that his regiment marches twenty-four miles on foot to York Town the next morning, expecting an onward movement toward Richmond. The tree toads, he confesses, make him think of home.

old: 25,000 troops at Hampton with one brigade. Steamer ran aground — had to transfer.
draft: Writing his brother Charles from a camp of some twenty-five thousand troops at Hampton, Va., Henry recounts a two-and-a-half-day boat passage whose steamer ran aground, forcing a transfer to reach shore. Confident in his bayonet drill, he nonetheless confesses he would rather be making sugar this spring than soldiering, and urges Charles not to let out the home sugar bush except to an honest man.

old: Pocket diary confirmed — "I have been keeping a pocket diary, write down everything that transpires from day to day. I have 28 dates.
draft: Writing from "Camp in field" as heavy musketry sounds off toward Yorktown, Henry tells his brother James he has been keeping a pocket diary with 28 dated entries recording "everything that transpires from day to day." Two days earlier his company double-quicked a mile expecting a fight; most of Co. D held together. He urges James toward West Point — yet still asks him to mind the cows and horse, hoping to be home next summer.

old: Pioneer duty at Yorktown — detailed as pioneers with axes, picks, shovels; building roads through woods for artillery. Rebels blocked roads.
draft: From a nameless "Camp in field" 16 miles from Hampton, Henry describes his regiment detailed as pioneers on the Sabbath — axes, picks, and shovels cutting new roads through woods the retreating rebels had blocked ahead of Yorktown. He records Gen. Gorman's cold counsel to keep cool in action "and not to mind if brother or cousin fell," then, watching Virginia trees in blossom, confesses the whole campaign "is all like a dream," wishing he were home for a sleigh ride.

old: Rebels at York Town "pretty well surrounded. " Rebel slave reported they left on double quick.
draft: Writing from camp sixteen miles from Fortress Monroe after his regiment took the boat from Alexandria, Henry reports the rebels holding Yorktown but "getting pretty well surrounded," and expects to march there any day for "a little skirmish." He passes along an enslaved man's account that the rebels fled "on a double quick" at news of the Union advance, then closes hoping to be home next June, "if the war is over."

old: Siege of Yorktown firsthand — 3 miles from rebel lines. Called into line for expected skirmish.
draft: Writing his brother Charles from camp three miles outside Yorktown, Henry relays his first secondhand battle reports — a repulsed rebel attack on a Union battery and a Vermont regiment so badly hit that one company was left with "only twenty." Continued across eight days, the letter closes with a rebel dawn attack on the 26th and a sharpshooter wounded. Henry confesses, "Nothing livens me up more than to hear the firing cannon."

old: Siege of Yorktown operations: Drums silenced and band doesn't play — fear of rebel shelling. attacked on picket — night before last, heavy musketry; rebels tried to drive pickets in but failed.
draft: From the Yorktown siege lines, Henry tells his brother James that the regiment's drums and band have gone silent for fear of drawing rebel shells, and recounts a midnight musketry alarm when the rebels failed to drive in the New York 2nd's pickets. Between gun inspections and four o'clock drills, he confesses he often thinks with pleasure of the spring he and James made maple sugar at home.

old: Sedgwick's Division, Gorman Brigade — unit identification confirmed. McClellan described: "Splendid looking fellow, smiling countenance, rides a fine horse," ~200 cavalry bodyguard.
draft: Writing from the siege lines near Yorktown, Henry pinpoints his place in the army — Sedgwick's Division, Gorman's Brigade — and watches a balloon rise daily to spy on the rebel works while McClellan, "a splendid looking fellow" with a 200-strong cavalry guard, rides past. Between picket duty on dark, dreary nights, his mind keeps drifting home to the horses, the cattle, and a farm with no one to see to it.

old: Pay and financial accounting: 2 months' pay; $20 home; boots $1 (Peter Guyan); sutler $1; cook 50¢; $3. Emerson Smith used all wages.
draft: Newly paid for two months at Fortress Monroe's Camp "Windfield Scott," Henry mails $20 home by express and itemizes every cent that remains. A Union tower rises opposite a nearby rebel fort, shelled daily, and the men sleep up before dawn braced for an attack. Henry notes the Sabbath goes unkept and trusts God "will not hold us accountable for what we cannot help."

old: Yorktown evacuated by rebels — Henry inside fortifications. "Immense and very strong.
draft: Writing from inside the evacuated Confederate fortifications at Yorktown — "immense and very strong," sandbags head-high — Henry marvels at works he calls the strongest he has seen. He recounts the hardest night of his soldiering: an all-night march in driving rain and deep mud, halting every ten paces. Buried shells left underfoot have already wounded some of his men.

old: West Point, VA — on York River, NOT the academy. 20-30 miles from Yorktown, ~30 from Richmond.
Cornwallis surrender spot — "pointed out to me. It was a great sight.
draft: Henry writes from West Point on the York River, twenty-five miles from Richmond, where the spot of Cornwallis's surrender was pointed out to him — "a great sight." Word of the 16th Regiment's skirmish, one company losing sixteen men, brings the war close: George Corbin and Royal, friends from home, shook his hand. He urges Mother to let the farm out on shares and spend the summer at Charlotte.

old: Camp Alton, West Point, VA — 34th Regt. Near unnamed river emptying into York River (likely Pamunkey or Mattaponi).

old: Battle of Fair Oaks aftermath — regiment lost 123 wounded and killed (papers said 150). D lost 2 killed and 10 wounded.
BATTLE OF FAIR OAKS — FIRSTHAND COMBAT ACCOUNT. "You can have no conception of how exciting it is to be in a battle.
One year of service — "A long year it has been to me. Twelve more months.
Henry's health in serious decline — dysentery "very bad," unable to do duty for over a week, Dr. every morning, quinine and pills.
FAIR OAKS — BAYONET CHARGE DETAIL: "pushed right in head first. " Came to bayonet charge at woods edge.
SEVEN DAYS RETREAT firsthand. was in a battle the last of June.
SEVEN DAYS RETREAT — extended detail. Sick ordered to hospital; McDonald came twice urging Henry to go; Henry stayed with the men.
GRAND REVIEW of Army of the Potomac at Harrison's Landing — "last Tuesday" (July 22). Near James River, within sight of gunboats.
